1.title: The Organization Practice in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module four: The Organization Practice in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two practices. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. three point two.one Apply the organization practice: project management team structure, role descriptions, commercial management approach, areas of focus of the key roles, effective management and techniques. three point two.two analyze whether an approach is effective and fit for purpose, considering the principles, the techniques and tailoring. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two practices (fifty-one percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose and the principles it serves
1.text: Purpose and the principles it serves. The organization practice sets up the accountability structure of the project: who is responsible for what, who decides, who reports to whom, and how the project works with its suppliers. Every project must represent three interests: business, user and supplier.

1.title: Purpose and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose and the principles it serves. The figure shows this: The project management team: corporate or programme level, directing, managing and delivering, with the three interests on the board.

1.title: Purpose and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose and the principles it serves. The main principle is define roles, responsibilities and relationships. The practice also serves manage by exception (delegation within tolerances), manage by stages (the board authorizes each stage and the team is reviewed at stage ends), focus on products (work goes to teams as work packages) and tailor. In the Official Book, products are in six point five, roles in Table six point four, management and techniques in six point two and six point three, and tailoring in six point seven.

1.title: The management products
1.text: The management products. All three are parts of the P I D. Project management team structure. Shows the roles, who holds them, and the reporting and delegation lines. Role descriptions. What each role is responsible for, its authority and the skills needed; each named person agrees to theirs. Commercial management approach. How the project works with suppliers: what is bought, contract and procurement arrangements, supplier performance and contract changes. Exam tip: The structure shows who, the role descriptions show what each person does, and the commercial management approach shows how suppliers fit. All three are in the P I D, not in the project log.

1.title: The team and the key roles
1.text: The team and the key roles. Corporate or programme. Who: Senior management. Focus: Mandate; appoints the executive; sets project tolerances. Directing. Who: Project board. Focus: Accountable for success; authorizes stages; decides on exceptions. Managing. Who: Project manager. Focus: Day-to-day management within tolerances. Delivering. Who: Team managers and team members. Focus: Produce the products in work packages.

1.title: The team and the key roles, continued
1.text: The team and the key roles. Executive. Single point of accountability; owns the business case; leads the board. Senior user. Speaks for the users: specifies their needs and ensures the products meet them. Senior supplier. Speaks for the supplier: commits supplier resources and is accountable for supplier quality. Project manager. Plans, controls and reports within tolerances; manages the team managers.

1.title: The team and the key roles, continued
1.text: The team and the key roles. Team manager. Delivers work packages to the agreed quality, time and cost. Project assurance. Independent checks for the board on the business, user and supplier interests. Change authority. Decides changes within the limits the board delegated. Project support. Administration: tools, records, reports and advice. Check Table six point four in the book when two roles seem to fit. Exam tip: Project assurance must be independent of the project manager. If the project manager, or someone who reports to the project manager, assures the work, the approach is not fit for purpose.

1.title: Effective management and techniques
1.text: Effective management and techniques. A balanced board. The business, user and supplier interests are each represented by someone with the authority to decide, the time to attend and the right seniority. One executive. A board small enough to decide. Delegation. The board delegates day-to-day management to the project manager within tolerances; the project manager delegates work to team managers through work packages; the board delegates small changes to a change authority within a limit. The board keeps its time for decisions. Choosing people. Pick for authority, competence, availability and conflicts of interest. Stakeholder analysis helps. Each person agrees to their role description.

1.title: Effective management and techniques, continued
1.text: Effective management and techniques. Communication lines. Everyone knows whom they report to; the supplier's team manager reports progress to the project manager. Commercial arrangements. The contract fits the stage structure and tolerances, supplier reporting matches project reporting, and the supplier's representative can commit resources. Techniques. A work breakdown structure and a responsibility matrix help allocate work and accountability. Review. Revisit the team at stage boundaries, when people and needs change. Exam tip: The change authority decides only inside the limit the board delegated. Above that limit, or when a tolerance is affected, the decision goes back to the project board.

1.title: Judging a scenario
1.text: Judging a scenario. Board balance. Effective: All three interests represented by people with authority. Red flag: Supplier absent; user voice cannot accept products. Principle: Define roles. Board size and time. Effective: Small board whose members attend. Red flag: Large committee; absent members. Principle: Define roles. Accountability. Effective: One executive; project manager works within tolerances. Red flag: Two owners; the project manager acts as executive. Principle: Define roles.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Delegation. Effective: Routine decisions with the project manager; small changes with the change authority. Red flag: Board approves routine items; project manager decides a tolerance breach. Principle: Manage by exception. Assurance. Effective: Independent of the project manager. Red flag: Project manager assures own work. Principle: Define roles. Commercial. Effective: Contract dates and reports fit stages and tolerances. Red flag: Contract ignores stages; supplier staff fill board roles. Principle: Manage by stages.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Records. Effective: Structure and role descriptions in the P I D, agreed by named people. Red flag: Roles assumed, never written down. Principle: Define roles.

2.title: Judging a scenario, continued
2.text: Judging a scenario. Tailoring. Small project: roles can be combined (the project manager as team manager and support) and the board kept small, but the three interests stay represented and assurance stays independent. Multi-party: several senior suppliers or users on the board, agreed spokespeople to keep it small, a team manager for each supplier and a formal commercial management approach. Agile delivery: a product owner may speak for the senior user and a delivery lead may act as team manager; the team organizes its own work inside work packages; the board and project manager roles stay. Exam tip: Tailoring may combine roles but never removes an interest or the independence of assurance. An option that drops the supplier or the user voice from the board because the project is small is wrong.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Marta Quinn proposes removing Lena Kovac from the Project Harbor board, because Delta Software is only a contractor and the board should hold Brightwater staff alone. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because the supplier interest needs a senior supplier able to commit supplier resources. Define roles, responsibilities and relationships requires the supplier interest to sit on the board through someone who can commit supplier resources, while the contract only covers commercial terms.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Short of staff, Sam Okafor plans to cover project assurance for the pilot stage of Project Harbor by reviewing his own plans. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Ask the board to arrange independent assurance, such as Aisha Bello. Project assurance must be independent of the project manager, so it comes from a board-appointed person and not from Sam or people who report to him.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. The board gave Tomas Reyes authority over changes up to ten thousand in Project Harbor. A request for a new payment feature would cost forty thousand. Who should decide it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: The project board, because the change exceeds the limit. The change authority decides only inside its delegated limit, so a larger change returns to the board under manage by exception.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Lena Kovac asks which Project Harbor document explains how Brightwater and Delta Software handle contract terms, supplier performance and contract changes. Which management product is it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: The commercial management approach. The commercial management approach in the P I D describes how the project works with its suppliers and contracts.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. On a small internal Brightwater project with no supplier, Sam proposes a small board that still covers the business, user and supplier interests, with himself also acting as team manager. He records this in the P I D. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Yes, because small boards and combined roles are fine if interests stay covered. Tailoring may combine roles and scale the board as long as the three interests stay represented and the decision is recorded in the P I D.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Brightwater signs a second supplier directly for the card-reader hardware of Project Harbor. What should Sam and Marta do about the project's organization? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Add a senior supplier for it and update the commercial management approach. A directly contracted supplier brings its own interest, so it needs its own representation and a commercial management approach that covers it.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the three project interests and who speaks for each. Answer: Business (the executive), user (the senior user) and supplier (the senior supplier). Question two. Who makes up the project board? Answer: The executive, the senior user or users, and the senior supplier or suppliers. Question three. Which three P I D products support the organization practice? Answer: The project management team structure, the role descriptions and the commercial management approach.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What must project assurance be? Answer: Independent of the project manager. Question five. What does the change authority do? Answer: Decides changes within the limits delegated by the board. Question six. Name the four levels of the project management team. Answer: Corporate or programme management, directing, managing and delivering.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Purpose: accountability structure: who decides, who reports to whom, how suppliers fit. Interests: business (executive), user (senior user), supplier (senior supplier). P I D products: team structure, role descriptions, commercial management approach. Levels: corporate or programme, directing, managing, delivering. Assurance: independent of the project manager; checks for all three interests. Change authority: decides inside the delegated limit; above it, the board decides. Red flags: missing interest, two owners, board decides routine matters, manager assures own work. Tailoring: combine roles and scale the board, never drop an interest or independence.
